title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 85
paragraphs: The Persians, then, had obtained possession of Sardis and had taken Croesus himself prisoner, after he had reigned fourteen years and had been besieged fourteen days, having fulfilled the oracle in that he had brought to an end his own great empire. The Persians then, having captured him, brought him into the presence of Cyrus. And Cyrus piled up a great pyre and made Croesus go up onto it bound in fetters, and with him twice seven sons of Lydians, whether it was that he meant to dedicate this offering as first-fruits of his victory to some god, or whether he wished to fulfill a vow, or else had heard that Croesus was a god-fearing man and so caused him to go up on the pyre because he wished to know if one of the divine powers would save him from being burned alive. This, they say, is what Cyrus did. But to Croesus, as he stood upon the pyre, there came, even in such evil plight, a memory of the saying of Solon, how he had declared with divine inspiration that no one of the living might be called happy. And when this thought came into his mind, they say that he sighed deeply and groaned aloud, having been long silent, and three times he uttered the name of Solon. Hearing this, Cyrus bade the interpreters ask Croesus who this person was on whom he called, and they came near and asked. Croesus for a time, it is said, kept silent when asked this, but afterwards, being pressed, he said: “One whom—more than much wealth—I should have wished all monarchs to have speech with.” Then, since his words were of doubtful meaning, they asked again what he meant; and as they were urgent with him and gave him no peace, he told how once Solon an Athenian had come, and having inspected all his wealth had made light of it with such and such words, and how it had all turned out for him according to what Solon had said, and that Solon had been speaking not at all with a view to Croesus in particular, but with a view to the whole human race and especially those who seem to themselves to be happy men. And while Croesus related these things, already the pyre was lighted and the edges of it all around were burning. Then they say that Cyrus, hearing from the interpreters what Croesus had said, changed his purpose and considered that he himself also was but a man, and that he was delivering another man—one who had been not inferior to himself in felicity—alive to the fire. Moreover he feared retribution, and reflected that nothing of what men possess is secure. Therefore, they say, he ordered his men to extinguish as quickly as possible the fire that was burning and to bring down Croesus and those who were with him from the pyre. But they, despite their efforts, were no longer able to master the flames.
